summary: As-cast Fe–30Mn–9Al–C–3Ni low-density steel, i.e. the conventionally cast (as-cast) condition of the Fe–30Mn–9Al–C–3Ni alloy studied in a paper devoted to selective laser melting (SLM) of the same composition. In this work the as-cast material serves purely as the control/benchmark state against which the SLM-printed samples (P-70, P-90, P-110, P-130, P-150) are compared; its room-temperature tensile behaviour was measured to quantify the property gain achievable by SLM relative to conventional casting.
composition: Nominal composition Fe–30Mn–9Al–C–3Ni (wt%), a low-density Fe–Mn–Al–C austenitic steel with Ni addition. The feedstock chemistry reported for the alloy (measured by ICP-OES on the PREP-prepared powder from which the alloy system was derived) is Mn 29.95, Al 8.63, C 1.20, Ni 3.45 and O 0.01 wt%, with Fe as balance. Mn stabilises austenite; Al provides the low-density/high-strength character of Fe–Mn–Al–C steels; C is the interstitial strengthening and κ-carbide-forming element; Ni is added to inhibit electrochemical activity and the initial micro-electro-coupling between second phases and austenite, thereby improving corrosion resistance. No separate composition measurement is reported specifically for the as-cast ingot, so this chemistry is taken as the alloy's nominal composition.
processing: The sample is the alloy in its conventional as-cast state. Per the paper it is described only as the "as-cast" Fe–30Mn–9Al–C–3Ni alloy used as the control/benchmark against the SLM-printed samples; no casting parameters (melt temperature, mould material, cooling medium, atmosphere, subsequent homogenisation or heat treatment) are reported for this condition. It therefore represents the process lineage "conventional casting" from which the SLM route (PREP powder + SLM at 70–150 W) is the novel alternative: the paper motivates SLM by noting that traditional routes such as casting, forging, rolling and annealing are costly, time-consuming and ill-suited to complex shapes in these hard Fe–Mn–Al–C alloys.
microstructure: No microstructural characterisation (XRD, EBSD, TEM, OM, density, hardness, porosity or surface roughness) is reported in the paper for the as-cast sample; all such data concern only the SLM-printed samples. The paper attributes the as-cast sample's inferior mechanical response to the absence of the grain-refinement strengthening produced by the rapid cooling of SLM, i.e. the cast condition is implicitly the coarser-grained state relative to the printed material.
properties: Room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing was performed on a dog-bone specimen (gauge length 25 mm, diameter 5 mm) on a Suns universal testing machine with a Reliant electronic extensometer at a loading rate of 1 mm/min. The as-cast Fe–30Mn–9Al–C–3Ni alloy exhibited a yield strength of 772.3 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of 879.0 MPa, an elongation of 20.53% and a reduction of area (Z) of 17.10%. Its engineering stress–strain curve rises steeply in the elastic regime and then plateaus between 800 and 900 MPa, terminating just past 20% strain, with no necking-type softening before the abrupt fracture drop. No hardness, physical, chemical or other service-property data are reported for this condition. Characterisation techniques applied to this sample: room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing only.
mechanisms: Conventional casting solidifies at a comparatively slow cooling rate, so the as-cast Fe–30Mn–9Al–C–3Ni alloy does not benefit from the rapid-cooling grain refinement that operates during SLM; this coarser-grained condition is the reason the cast sample shows both lower strength and lower plasticity than the SLM-printed samples.

Because SLM solidification is much faster than casting, the printed samples develop finer grains (grain-refinement strengthening), which raises strength and ductility simultaneously; measured against that mechanism, the as-cast state represents the un-refined baseline whose yield strength (772.3 MPa), tensile strength (879.0 MPa), elongation (20.53%) and reduction of area (17.10%) are the lowest of all conditions compared.

The as-cast sample's stress–strain behaviour — a long plateau between 800 and 900 MPa ending just past 20% strain — reflects a comparatively low work-hardening/tensile capacity relative to the SLM samples, whose plateaus lie above 1000 MPa and extend to much larger strains.
conclusions: The as-cast Fe–30Mn–9Al–C–3Ni alloy is the benchmark against which the first-time SLM manufacture of this low-density steel is assessed. It is the weakest of all the compared conditions: its tensile strength (879.0 MPa) lies well below every SLM sample, and its elongation (20.53%) and reduction of area (17.10%) are the lowest of the group. The comparison demonstrates that SLM processing of this Fe–Mn–Al–C–Ni low-density steel raises both strength and ductility above the conventionally cast state, an improvement the authors attribute to the grain-refinement strengthening caused by rapid cooling during SLM; the best SLM condition (P-110) reached YS 887.1 MPa, UTS 1076.8 MPa, EL 40.80% and 294 HV. The result supports the study's overall message that SLM is a viable route to Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steel components with complex geometry and superior comprehensive mechanical properties.

The as-cast sample's tensile strength (879.0 MPa) is below all five SLM-printed samples, and its elongation (20.53%) and reduction of area (17.10%) are the lowest of the compared group, making it the weakest condition in the study.

No microstructural (XRD/EBSD/TEM/OM), density, hardness, porosity or surface-roughness characterisation is reported in the paper for the as-cast sample; all such data pertain only to the SLM-printed samples.
The as-cast sample's fracture surface was not examined; fracture-surface analysis (ductile dimples, lack-of-fusion particles, cleavage and cracks) is reported only for the SLM-printed samples.
